title: Linguine alle Vongole in Bianco
subtitle: clams and linguine in white wine and garlic
excerpt: Linguine alle vongole in bianco is the clean white version: live clams steamed open in white wine and garlic, tossed with linguine and finished with parsley and good olive oil. No tomato, no cream. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Linguine alle vongole in bianco is one of the defining dishes of Neapolitan and Campanian coastal cooking. The white version predates the in rosso version and appears in 19th-century Neapolitan cookbooks as a simple preparation of clams with wine, garlic, and oil. Pellegrino Artusi, La scienza in cucina (1891, public domain in Italy), documents clams cooked in this basic manner. The pairing with linguine rather than spaghetti is a southern Italian convention; both shapes are used throughout Italy and both work well. The dish is served without cheese: Parmesan on shellfish pasta is considered wrong in Italian cooking, and the clam liquor provides its own seasoning.

glossaryTerms.definition: The briny liquid released by clams as they open during cooking. It is intensely flavoured and salty and forms the base of the sauce. Do not add extra salt until after the clams have opened and you have tasted the sauce.

content.text: Linguine alle vongole in bianco is the purer of the two clam pasta versions. No tomato intervenes between the

and the pasta. The sauce is just the liquid the clams release as they open in the wine, combined with the olive oil and enriched with a ladle of starchy pasta water. The flavour is bracingly saline and clean.

Timing is critical. The pasta and the clams need to be ready within a minute of each other. Start the pasta once the sauce is in the pan, and have the clams ready to add before the pasta finishes. Everything gets tossed together in the pan for the final cooking.

items.prepNote: live, in shell, purged 30 minutes in salted water

content.text: Purge the clams in cold salted water for at least 30 minutes. Drain and discard any open shells that do not close when tapped.

Bring a large pot of well-salted water to the boil. Start cooking {{pasta-dried}} of linguine 3 minutes before the clams are due to finish: it needs to be 2 minutes short of al dente when the clams open.
Heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil in a large saute pan over a medium heat. Add {{garlic}} of garlic and chilli flakes if using; cook for 1 minute until fragrant but not brown. Turn the heat to high.

Add the drained clams and {{dry-white-wine}} of white wine. Cover immediately and cook for 3 to 4 minutes, shaking the pan once or twice, until all the clams are open. Discard any that remain closed. Reserve 150 ml of pasta cooking water.

Drain the linguine and add to the clam pan. Toss over a high heat for 1 to 2 minutes with a splash of pasta water until the pasta is coated and the sauce has emulsified slightly. Add {{parsley-flat}} of parsley and a drizzle of olive oil. Serve immediately.

items.symptom: Sauce is watery and does not coat the pasta
items.cause: Not enough tossing time, or pasta water not added
items.fix: Toss vigorously in the pan for a full 2 minutes. A splash of starchy pasta water helps the oil emulsify into a sauce.
Clams are done the moment they open. Turn the heat off and add the pasta immediately to stop them cooking further.

items.cause: Clam liquor is already salty; added salt on top
items.fix: Do not season until after the clams have opened. Taste the sauce before adding any salt.

content.text: This is coastal southern Italy at its most direct: pasta and shellfish and olive oil and wine. It appears on restaurant menus along the entire Campanian coastline, from Naples south to Cilento, and is one of the dishes most closely associated with summer evenings near the sea. The in bianco version is austere in a way that the in rosso version is not: it asks that the clam liquor alone carries the flavour, which it does when the clams are fresh and properly prepared. No Parmesan. No cream. Nothing that does not belong.
